title: What does the ISM Code require shipping companies to do about crew familiarization and training?
seoTitle: ISM Code section 6: crew and training
description: ISM Code section 6 on resources and personnel: master qualification, familiarization, identifying training needs and working language, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Section 6 of the International Maritime Organization's ISM Code, mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX, requires the company to ensure the master is qualified and conversant with the safety management system, to man each ship with qualified, certificated and medically fit seafarers, to give new and transferred personnel proper familiarization before they take up safety duties, to identify and provide any training the SMS needs, and to give information in a working language the crew understands.
keyTakeaways: The ISM Code was adopted in 1993 by resolution A.741(18) and became mandatory on July 1, 1998 through the 1994 SOLAS amendments that created chapter IX.

Section 6 has seven paragraphs: master qualification and support (6.1), manning (6.2), familiarization (6.3), knowledge of rules (6.4), identifying training needs (6.5), working language (6.6) and effective communication (6.7).

Paragraph 6.2 was replaced by resolution MSC.353(92), in force from January 1, 2015, adding that each ship must be appropriately manned to encompass all aspects of maintaining safe operations on board.
Section 6 does not prescribe courses or hours: the company must establish procedures, and auditors test whether those procedures exist and work.
Internal safety audits ashore and on board must take place at intervals not exceeding twelve months, which is where weak familiarization and training records are usually found first.
jurisdiction: International (IMO), applied by flag States under SOLAS chapter IX
regulator: International Maritime Organization (IMO); flag State administrations and the recognized organizations acting for them
appliesTo: Companies operating ships to which SOLAS chapter IX applies, including passenger ships, tankers, bulk carriers, other cargo ships and mobile offshore drilling units of 500 gross tonnage and upwards on international voyages
Masters, who must be qualified for command and fully conversant with the company's SMS
Designated persons ashore and shore-based managers who run the SMS
Crewing managers and ship managers to whom ISM-related tasks are delegated

sections.heading: Where do the ISM Code's personnel requirements come from?

blocks.text: They come from section 6, "Resources and personnel", of the International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention (the ISM Code). According to [IMO](https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/HumanElement/Pages/ISMCode.aspx), the Code in its current form was adopted in 1993 by resolution A.741(18) and was made mandatory with the entry into force, on July 1, 1998, of the 1994 amendments to the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), which introduced chapter IX.

The Code applies in stages. The recitals to [Regulation (EC) No 336/2006](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32006R0336) record that it became mandatory on July 1, 1998 for companies operating passenger ships, oil tankers, chemical tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers and cargo high-speed craft of 500 gross tonnage and upwards on international voyages, and on July 1, 2002 for other cargo ships and mobile offshore drilling units of 500 gross tonnage and upwards.

IMO describes the Code as deliberately broad: "no two shipping companies or shipowners are the same", so it sets principles and objectives rather than detailed prescriptions. IMO also states that "it is the commitment, competence, attitudes and motivation of individuals at all levels that determines the end result." Section 6 is where that principle becomes a set of company duties about people.

sections.heading: What does each paragraph of section 6 require?

blocks.text: Section 6 places seven duties on the company, which the Code defines as the owner or the organization that has assumed responsibility for operating the ship. The wording below follows the Code text as reproduced in Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 336/2006, with paragraph 6.2 as replaced by resolution MSC.353(92).

items: **6.1 The master.** The company should ensure the master is properly qualified for command, fully conversant with the company's SMS, and given the necessary support so that the master's duties can be safely performed.

**6.2 Manning.** Each ship must be manned with qualified, certificated and medically fit seafarers in accordance with national and international requirements, and appropriately manned to encompass all aspects of maintaining safe operations on board.

**6.3 Familiarization.** The company should establish procedures so that new personnel, and personnel transferred to new assignments related to safety and protection of the environment, are given proper familiarization with their duties. Instructions that must be provided prior to sailing should be identified, documented and given.
**6.4 Knowledge of rules.** All personnel involved in the SMS should have an adequate understanding of relevant rules, regulations, codes and guidelines.

**6.5 Training needs.** The company should establish and maintain procedures for identifying any training which may be required in support of the SMS, and ensure that training is provided for all personnel concerned.
**6.6 Working language.** Ship's personnel should receive relevant information on the SMS in a working language or languages understood by them.
**6.7 Communication.** Ship's personnel should be able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties related to the SMS.

blocks.text: Two features matter for a training manager. First, the duties are written as procedures the company must establish, not courses it must buy. Second, paragraph 6.5 is a [training needs analysis](/glossary/training-needs-analysis) obligation in all but name: the company must have a repeatable way to find the gaps between what the SMS requires and what its people can do.

sections.heading: How did the 2013 amendment change the manning duty?

blocks.text: It widened it from certification to capacity. [Resolution MSC.353(92)](https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/OurWork/HumanElement/Documents/353(92).pdf), adopted on June 21, 2013 and in force from January 1, 2015, replaced paragraph 6.2 so that each ship must be both manned with qualified, certificated and medically fit seafarers and "appropriately manned in order to encompass all aspects of maintaining safe operations on board", with a footnote to the IMO Principles of minimum safe manning in resolution A.1047(27).

The same resolution inserted a new paragraph 12.2: the company should periodically verify whether all those undertaking delegated ISM-related tasks are acting in conformity with the company's responsibilities under the Code. Where crewing or training is outsourced to a manning agent, that verification duty stays with the company. It also added a footnote to section 4 pointing to IMO's guidance on the qualifications, training and experience necessary for the role of the designated person (MSC-MEPC.7/Circ.6).

sections.heading: What does proper familiarization look like to an auditor?

blocks.text: It looks like a documented procedure, a ship-specific checklist and a signed record for each person, completed before the person takes up safety duties. Paragraph 6.3 does two things: it requires familiarization for both new joiners and people moving to a new safety-related assignment, and it requires the company to identify which instructions must be given before sailing and to document that they were given.

The interim certification rules show how seriously the Code treats this. Under paragraph 14.4, an Interim Safety Management Certificate may only be issued after verification that, among other things, the master and officers are familiar with the SMS and planned arrangements for its implementation, instructions identified as essential are provided prior to sailing, and relevant SMS information has been given in a working language understood by the ship's personnel. An interim certificate is valid for up to six months.

Familiarization is distinct from STCW certification. A seafarer can hold every certificate required by the [STCW Convention](/regulations/stcw-seafarer-training-requirements) and still be unfamiliar with a particular ship's equipment and emergency procedures. A well-built [safety induction](/guides/how-to-build-a-safety-induction) for each vessel type is the usual way companies meet paragraph 6.3.

sections.heading: How is compliance with section 6 checked?

blocks.text: Through the company's own audits and through flag State certification. Since resolution [MSC.273(85)](https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/OurWork/HumanElement/Documents/273(85).pdf) entered into force on July 1, 2010, paragraph 12.1 requires internal safety audits on board and ashore at intervals not exceeding twelve months, which may be exceeded by not more than three months in exceptional circumstances.

Externally, the company holds a Document of Compliance valid for up to five years and subject to annual verification within three months of each anniversary date, and each ship holds a Safety Management Certificate valid for up to five years with at least one intermediate verification. Where only one intermediate verification is carried out on a five-year certificate, it takes place between the second and third anniversary dates.

IMO's [Revised guidelines on the implementation of the ISM Code by Administrations](https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/es/OurWork/HumanElement/Documents/A%2030-Res.1118%20-%20English.pdf), resolution A.1118(30) adopted on December 6, 2017, tell auditors to collect objective evidence through interviews and examination of documents, with observation of activities where necessary. In practice, a seafarer who cannot explain the emergency procedures for their own station is evidence against paragraphs 6.3 and 6.5, whatever the training records say. The same guidelines require ISM auditors themselves to complete at least four supervised training audits, including at least one company audit and one shipboard audit.

sections.heading: How do national regimes use the ISM Code?

blocks.text: Many flag States apply the Code beyond its SOLAS scope. In the European Union, Regulation (EC) No 336/2006 makes the Code applicable to ships flying a Member State flag and to certain ships operating domestic services. In Australia, the Australian Maritime Safety Authority's [safety management systems page](https://www.amsa.gov.au/vessels-operators/domestic-commercial-vessels/safety-management-systems) says Class 1, 2 and 3 domestic commercial vessels may meet their SMS obligation either through Schedule 1 of Marine Order 504 or through ISM Code Part A, with some added Schedule 1 paragraphs.

That flexibility matters to training teams in mixed fleets: one familiarization and training-needs procedure written to section 6 can often serve both international and domestic vessels. Australian domestic crew rules are covered in [AMSA domestic commercial vessel crew requirements](/regulations/amsa-domestic-commercial-vessel-crew-requirements).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each section 6 paragraph as an obligation linked to the SMS procedures that discharge it and to the roles and ship types it applies to. Familiarization items and SMS training needs then become assessment points with evidence attached, so a company can show an ISM auditor which seafarers are familiarized with which ship and why each training item exists.

faqs.q: Does the ISM Code specify how many hours of familiarization a seafarer needs?
faqs.a: No. Paragraph 6.3 requires the company to establish procedures for proper familiarization and to identify, document and give the instructions needed before sailing. The content and duration are for the company to set based on the ship, the role and the risks, and auditors check that the procedure exists and is followed.

faqs.q: Is the training in paragraph 6.5 the same as STCW training?
faqs.a: Not exactly. STCW sets certification standards for seafarers. Paragraph 6.5 requires the company to identify any training needed to support its own SMS, which can include company procedures, ship-specific equipment and lessons from incidents. STCW certificates help satisfy paragraph 6.2 on manning, but they do not discharge paragraph 6.5 by themselves.

faqs.q: Can a company delegate crewing and training to a manning agency?
faqs.a: It can delegate the tasks but not the responsibility. Paragraph 12.2, added by resolution MSC.353(92) from January 1, 2015, requires the company to periodically verify that everyone undertaking delegated ISM-related tasks is acting in conformity with the company's responsibilities under the Code.

faqs.q: How often does the ISM Code require internal audits?
faqs.a: Paragraph 12.1, as amended by resolution MSC.273(85) from July 1, 2010, requires internal safety audits on board and ashore at intervals not exceeding twelve months. In exceptional circumstances the interval may be exceeded by not more than three months.
